sweep_summary: Lycian A is not in the catalog. The single title-search hit (Gabriel 1961, 'Akzent und Vokalismus der Mundarten von Dornbirn, Lustenau und Hohenems') is a Glottolog mis-assignment: the record's own language code field says 'Lycian A [xlc] (computerized assignment from \"vokalismus\")', and the paper is about Vorarlberg Alemannic German dialects -- relevance another language or variety, priority none. Kloekhorst 2008 Kadmos DOI returned an empty page; de Gruyter 405; Leiden repository ECONNRESET; Semantic Scholar API 429; The best first-hand statements are the ones already held by the project from our earlier reading and re-read here: Melchert 2004 (Cambridge Encyclopedia, p. 596, sec. 3.2.2) -- 'our knowledge of Lycian accent is indirect, being based almost entirely on the effects of the syncope' -- and Kloekhorst 2013 (Jazyki mira 20, pp. 135 and 143), who infers unstressed-vowel syncope and a mobile accent in the mahana- paradigm. Reading: no fixed word-stress position is known for Lycian; accent is reconstructed indirectly and appears mobile. Highest-priority unread print sources: Hajnal 1995 'Der lykische Vokalismus' (Graz) pp. 175ff. and Melchert 1994 'Anatolian Historical Phonology' p. 318ff./326 (Google Books snippet already shows 'we have no direct evidence for the synchronic Lycian accent.. indirect effects such as syncope suggest that in general the place of the PA accent is preserved').

new_statements.rule_in_words: No synchronic rule for the position of the Lycian word accent can be stated: the alphabet does not mark accent and the language is known only from inscriptions. What is said about accent is reconstructed from prehistoric syncope of unaccented vowels (both before and after the accented syllable), which is taken to show that Lycian by and large continued the free, paradigmatically mobile Proto-Anatolian accent (Melchert 1994:326 snippet: 'in general the place of the PA accent is preserved'; Kloekhorst 2013:143 infers accent alternating between syllables within one paradigm). Melchert 2004 warns the whole inference is at risk of circularity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Melchert 1994 (snippets pp. 320, 327): assumed rightward accent shift in univerbation of preverbs with verbs, explaining reduced first syllables of several preverbs; proclitic nte 'into' with final accent 'due to proclisis' (Melchert 1993:249, 251). Eichner 1993 proposed an accent analysis partly from Lycian verse (not seen).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word including proclitics is the domain of the related umlaut rule (Melchert 2004:595); accent statements are diachronic inferences about the prehistoric word, not observations of citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Lycian proper ('Lycian A', lyci1241); Melchert 2004 explicitly confines his phonology to Lycian A and treats Milyan ('Lycian B', mily1238) separately; Kloekhorst 2013 likewise (Milyan has its own chapter by Shevoroshkin in the same volume). Accent is not written in the Lycian alphabet; every claim about its position is a reconstruction from prehistoric syncope (and, in Eichner 1993, from verse).

new_statements.quote: Lycian shows widespread prehistoric syncope. For two independent attempts at a comprehensive description see Melchert 1994a:318ff. and Hajnal 1995:175ff. The broad agreement between the two accounts, despite differences in detail, suggests that their general thrust is correct. Nevertheless, since our knowledge of Lycian accent is indirect, being based almost entirely on the effects of the syncope, the risk of circularity of argument is high, and neither analysis should be taken as remotely definitive.
new_statements.citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 2004. "Lycian". In R. D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, 591-600. Cambridge: CUP. Section 3.2.2 Syncope, p. 596.
new_statements.locator: p. 596, sec. 3.2.2 (scanned file lines 236-243; page image scanned/)
new_statements.reading: There is no direct evidence for the position of the Lycian word accent; it is inferred only from prehistoric syncope of unaccented vowels, and Melchert warns that even the reconstructions (Melchert 1994 AHP p. 318ff; Hajnal 1995 p. 175ff.) are not definitive. Kloekhorst 2013 (Jazyki mira vol. 20, 'Likijskij jazyk', p. 135, held by the project as lines 6496-6498) says the same in Russian: 'Точные условия такой синкопы не ясны, но она, без сомнения, должна была быть результатом безударности того или иного гласного' ('The exact conditions of this syncope are unclear, but it was without doubt the result of the unstressed status of one or another vowel'), and on p. 143 infers a mobile accent within the mahana- 'god' paradigm (nom. pl. mãhãi with second-syllable syncope = unaccented, vs dat. pl. mahãna without syncope = accented). Net: Lycian A has NO fixed, positionally statable word stress in the literature -- the accent is reconstructed as lexically/morphologically mobile (inherited Proto-Anatolian position), and the language should be coded as 'no determinable/unknown' or 'lexical (reconstructed) accent', not as any fixed-position type.
